Photography Guide

Full-moon desert photography, honestly planned

The bright Milky Way core is below the horizon in February and the Feb 20 full moon floods the sky. The trip can still produce excellent work—just not the classic core-over-Joshua-tree frame.

Golden hour

sunset about 5:34–5:36 p.m.

  • Cap Rock: backlit trees and easy silhouettes.
  • Cholla Garden: arrive 60 minutes early and stay on the path.
  • Keys View: layer ridges only on a clear, low-wind evening.

Moonlit landscape

use the moon as key light

  • Expose foreground first; bracket highlights on the lunar disc.
  • Start around ISO 400–1600, f/2.8–4, 2–10 sec and inspect histogram.
  • Shoot east-facing subjects after moonrise; watch your own shadow.

Winter night sky

Orion, star trails and the faint winter band

  • Use 14–24mm, sturdy tripod, manual focus and 2-second delay.
  • For trails: 100–200 frames at 15–20 sec with intervalometer.
  • Turn off cabin/vehicle lights and never block traffic at a pullout.

Milky Way truth

Core seasonRoughly March/April through September
This tripCore below horizon; 87–100% moon
Best dark alternativeMove near a new moon, preferably Apr–Aug
A Feb 5–9 dark-moon shift would improve winter stars but still would not create a visible galactic core.

Field kit

Bodies/lensesWide fast lens + 70–200 for moon compression
SupportTripod, intervalometer, red headlamp
ColdSpare batteries inside jacket
Scout compositions in daylight and remain at paved pullouts or designated areas after dark.
